study.title: 2 Samuel 24 The census, the judgment, and the altar that interrupts the plague
study.overview: This chapter shows David leading Israel to an act which he later recognizes as sin: to order the census of the people. The narrative highlights both human responsibility and the sovereignty of God, which allows judgment and also interrupts it. The center of the chapter is not only punishment, but the divine mercy that leads David to repentance, intercession and the construction of an altar in the place where death is detained. The end result is that the plague ceases because the Lord has compassion on the earth.

outline.title: David orders the census and the people are counted
outline.explanation: The wrath of the Lord against Israel appears as a backdrop, and David tells all the people, from the traditional limits of the earth, Dan to Beersheba. Joab disagrees and tries to dissuade the king, but the royal order prevails. The count takes nine months and twenty days and ends with high numbers of warriors fit for war, indicating that the focus of the census was on military force.

outline.title: David confesses sin and chooses to fall into the hands of the Lord
outline.explanation: After the census, David is taken from remorse and confesses having acted madly. God sends Gad with three judgment options: famine, escape from enemies or pestilence. David chooses the punishment coming from the hand of the Lord, trusting in his many mercies, and then comes a devastating plague upon Israel.

outline.title: God's mercy holds the angel and David seeks solution
outline.explanation: When the angel approaches Jerusalem, the Lord holds destruction. David sees the angel and takes the blame again, asking that the punitive hand fall upon him and his house, and not upon the people. Gad then guides him up and raise an altar in the eira of Araúna, the Jebusus, showing that the answer to judgment includes adoration and atonement.

outline.title: The altar is built and the plague ceases
outline.explanation: Araúna offers materials and animals to the king, but David insists on buying the eira, refusing to offer the Lord something that costs him nothing. David builds the altar, presents burnt offerings and peace offerings, and the text concludes by saying that the Lord was appeased with the earth and the plague ceased.

study.context: The chapter describes a census of the entire territory of Israel, using the traditional formula of Dã to Berseba to indicate the entirety of the land. The notes report that the count had strong connection with military aptitude and that a census could be seen as intrusion and as preparation for war or taxation. It is also important to the setting of the eira de Araúna, an outdoor threshing space, where the altar is erected; the place will be remembered later as associated with the temple.
study.theology: Theologically, the chapter teaches that leadership sin reaches the entire people and that human pride can deform even apparently administrative decisions. The narrative also shows that divine justice is not arbitrary: God sends judgment, but grants room for repentance and a sacrificial mediation. David does not try to justify himself; he confesses guilt and accepts that the punishment comes from the hand of the Lord, acknowledging that divine mercy is preferable to purely human treatment. The final altar points out that reconciliation with God involves sacrifice, obedient worship, and recognition of the cost of sin. In Protestant evangelical reading, this echoes the pattern that forgiveness and pacification with God depend on his merciful initiative, although the text here remains within the sacrificial economy of the Old Testament.

scholarViews.insight: The census is understood as something linked to military confidence and possibly motivated by pride or preparation for war; the term used indicates incitement to error.
David's choice to fall into the hands of the Lord shows that he prefers divine correction to human violence, trusting in God's great mercy.

questions: What, in David's attitude, reveals confidence in human power rather than dependence on God?
Why does David prefer to face God's judgment to fall into the hands of men?
What does it mean, in practice, to refuse to worship God with something that has no personal cost?
study.practice: Examine the motivations behind your decisions, especially when you involve control, numbers, results, or human safety. When you perceive sin, confess without excuses and seek God's mercy with real repentance. In Christian worship and service, refuse easy offerings and without inner sacrifice: offer the Lord concrete obedience, time, resources and humility. Also learn from David to intercede for others when someone's mistake affects many people, asking God to have compassion on the earth.
study.uncertainty: The biblical text of 2 Samuel does not explain why the wrath of the Lord was kindled against Israel, and the notes also recognize this as unknown. In addition, the numerical differences in parallel passages of Chronicles are not definitively resolved here; the chapter of 2 Samuel presents its own numbers and the study should not force harmonizations not explained by the notes.
